preamble: Anaptyxis (svarabhakti) inserts a neutral vowel [ə] between consonants, most often to split a liquid or nasal from a following consonant at the end of a syllable. The same configuration, /l/ or /r/ followed by a labial or dorsal consonant, triggers it independently in Irish and Irish English (film [ˈfɪləm]), in Dutch (melk [ˈmɛlək]) and in Irish (gorm [ˈɡɔɾˠəmˠ]). Some American English speakers also break the /θl/ cluster in athlete.

languageExamples.language: English (Irish, Scottish and some dialectal varieties)

examples.note: Svarabhakti vowel in /lm/, characteristic of Irish English and also found in Scottish and some northern English speech.
Epenthetic schwa breaking /θl/ in some American speakers; widely regarded as non-standard.

An epenthetic [ə] may be inserted between /l, r/ and a word-final /m, n, p, k, f, x/, also in compounds (melkboer [ˈmɛləkbuːr] 'milkman'). The pronunciation occurs in all varieties, including standard Dutch.

/ə/ breaks a cluster of /r, l, n/ followed by a labial or dorsal consonant other than /p, k/ after a short vowel, as in fearg [ˈfʲaɾˠəɡ] 'anger' and colm [ˈkɔl̪ˠəmˠ] 'dove'. It does not apply after long vowels (téarma [ˈtʲeːɾˠmˠə]).

sources: Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Cambridge University Press.
Collins, B., & Mees, I. M. (2003). The Phonetics of English and Dutch (5th ed.). Brill.
Ó Siadhail, M. (1989). Modern Irish: Grammatical Structure and Dialectal Variation. Cambridge University Press.
